EDWARD L. STEVENS, CHI '99
By Benjamin T.
SUCCEEDING
a long list of
distinguished and nationally
known brothers, Edward L. Stevens,
Chi '99, served as President of the
Executive Council of Psi Upsilon
from 1928 to 1933. His immediate
predecessor was Earl D. Babst,
Iota-Phi '93.
Brother Stevens was born in
Rome, New York, on June M, 1877,
and received his early education at
the Rome Free Academy, from
which he graduated in 1894. Enter
ing Cornell University with the
Class of 1899, Brother Stevens was
a prominent and active member of
that class during his undergraduate
years, being elected to Phi Beta
Kappa in 1898 and to Sphinx Head,
a Senior Honorary Society, in his
senior year. After receiving his
Bachelor of Arts degree in 1899,
Brother Stevens attended the Cor
nell Law School from which he was
graduated in 1902. From 1902 to
1920, he was a prominent member
of the Bar of New York City and a
partner in the law firm of Sackett,
Chapman and Stevens. Always an
active member of the Cornell Uni
versity Club of New York City, it
was but natural that Brother Ste
vens be elected to head the Cor
nellian Council. Largely due to his
efforts as President of the Cornel
lian Council from 1918 to 1920, the
endowment of Cornell University
was substantially increased.
In 1921, Brother Stevens returned
to the vicinity of his birth, and lo
cated in Delhi, New York, where
now he practices law.
BuKTON, Chi '21
Brother Stevens is a member of
one of Psi U's oldest and most il
lustrious families. He is the son of
Edward L. Stevens, Theta '55, and
two of his brothers are members of
the Chi Chapter, Stoddard M. Ste
vens, Chi '85 and Harold B. Stevens,
Chi '02. Two sons, Edward L.
Stevens, Psi '30 and Lyndon H.
Stevens, Chi '39, continue the Psi
U tradition. Brother Stevens is also
an uncle of Stoddard M. Stevens,
Jr., Chi '14 and George May Ste
vens, Chi '16.
Few members of the fraternity
have been as intensely interested in
its continued success as Edward L.
Stevens. Serving as a member of the
Executive Council for a period of
twenty-two years from 1911 to 1933,
the last five years of which he was
President, Brother Stevens brought
about more frequent and more thor
ough Chapter visits by members of
the Council. Through his visita
tions practically every active chap
ter in the Fraternity knew him well
and often. The message he carried
on those missions has inspired and
helped mould the lives of many in
coming delegations in our Chapters
throughout the United States and
Canada, and his sincerity of purpose
was recognized by hundreds of un
dergraduates who were fortunate
enough to know him. He always
sought to make Psi U initiates re
alize that membership in the Frater
nity is an expression of faith in them
on the part of their elder brothers,
which they must justify by loyal
service, not an earned honor, but

rather a privilege and opportunity,
and that snobbishness is a mark of
a shallow and selfish nature. He en
deavored to keep ever before Psi U
Chapters, that their chief purpose
and very reason for their existence,
is loyalty to their respective col
leges and universities, keeping this
same basic idea clearly in the minds
of the members of college and uni
versity administrations.
"Ned," as he is affectionately
called by the older members of the
Fraternity, is known for his interest
in the well-being of the whole Psi U
family. In recent years he has en
deavored to make each Psi U Chap
ter realize that it is part of an or
ganization, which is greater than
any of its constituent parts. In these
days of social change and attempts
on the part of some to challenge the
existence of fraternities, this service
has been especially valuable, and
especially appreciated by those who
have experienced the benefits of Psi
Upsilon.
Those of us who were privileged
to hear the address of Brother Ste
vens, at the banquet, concluding
the Centennial celebration in 1933,
recall particularly his scholarly ap
peal to the youth of Psi Upsilon.
Brother Stevens concluded his ad
dress as follows :
"Youth is the most important thing
in the world," as dear old Barry Mohun
told Chief Justice Taft in securing his
presence, despite his doctor's orders, at
our great Washington Convention four
years ago. Youth and the faith of youth
founded Psi Upsilon, have maintained
her great traditions and have kept her
standards high. We older men must not
disappoint that faith. As individuals, our
efiforts to help our younger Brothers to
get a start, in this strange, groping new
world around us, may seem pitiably in
effectual ; but there are more than twelve
thousand of us. The hope of America,
and the World, is in her picked young
men. After the World War, we recog
nized that fact, but carried it too far
and placed upon young executives bur
dens too heavy for their limited experi
ence. But can we afford any longer to go
to the opposite extreme? There are
many young men, about to go out from
our Chapter halls next June, who need
only the opportunity of a start, to
prove their value. We must not waste
this great source of strength; above all,
we must not change their faith to cyni
cism.
And our younger Brothers, on their
part, must be ready to answer any call,
recognizing it as an opportunity for
service as well as for a livelihood.
Brother Taft reminded our undergradu
ates, in his great talk at the Washington
Convention, of the dreadful waste of
opportunity in the college by many
young men. "Three things," he said,
"will make them useful to themselves
and to the world. One is work and hard
work; another is self-denial; and a third
is the discipline of character the prac
tice of the others brings about." That
advice was important in 1929; surely it
is vital today.
Brothers of the then and now, I have
faith in Psi Upsilon. Her life, I believe,
will go on, useful as of old, so long as
her sons continue to serve her ideals,
simply and sincerely, in the spirit of our
Founders.
Probably the greatest celebration
ever held by Psi Upsilon was the
Centennial Convention held in No
vember 1933, at the Theta. At
tended by nine hundred sons of Psi
U, Brother Edward L. Stevens was
elected permanent President of that
Convention, and no one was more
responsible for the success of that
never to be forgotten spectacle.

"And when our little ones come on.
We'll brand them all Psi Upsilon."
THE
Editor has made a deter
mined effort to discover just
how many of our undergraduate
brothers have Psi U relatives. The
associate editor of The Diamond

out a questionnaire giving this infor

all but the Rho. The length of the

Brother Edward L. Stevens, Chi
'99, a former President of the Ex
ecutive Council and a member of a
distinguished Psi U family, wrote as
follows for the January, 1936, issue
of The Diamond :
"All other things being equal,
however, I believe that a fine legacy
has a
slight edge over another fine
boy whose family is new to Psi Up
silon's roster. His environment and
heredity have combined to give him
a love for our Fraternity which it
will take the other pledges some
little time to acquire. He is intel
ligently interested in Psi U history
and tradition, which are part of his
own
family history and tradition.
Furthermore, he realizes that Psi
Upsilon is not just a
college club,
but a Uving brotherhood of friends,
whose fundamental ideals have met
the test of a century's proving. If
he is the right kind of a boy, he will
look on this background as giving
him something fine to share with his
delegation mates; as they, doubt
less, have something fine to share
with him, something in which they
have a better start than he. He
should realize, too, that they will
soon gain that love and special in
terest, with which he has been
lucky enough to start. Only a legacy
far below our Fraternity's standards
would let his Psi U antecedents
make him smug or cocky, or give
him the complacent feeling that he
has arrived and needs do little to
justify his election to Psi Upsilon."
Two hundred and thirty-nine un
dergraduate Brothers and pledges
from all the chapters, the Rho ex
cepted, have a Psi Upsilon heritage.
There are about 975 members in col
lege today. Far out in front is the

is unknown. In other words, 349 Psi

KENYON COLLEGE HOST
TO 1938 CONVENTION
KENYON College, which com
bines its 113 years of fine, vigor
ous tradition with one of the most
progressive, most alert educational
policies in the country, will be host
to the 1938 Convention of Psi Upsi
lon on April 18, 19, 20. At that time
the Iota will welcome representa
tives of every active Chapter of our
Fraternity. The Conventions of
1867, 1888, and 1910 were held with
the Iota.
Situated atop its historic "Hill"
under the towering trees planted
nearly 100 years ago by Philander
Chase, the founder of Kenyon Col
lege, and with the picturesque Kokosing River winding far below, this
oldest men's college in the Midwest
will present a scene of beauty to Psi
Upsilon which will surely be long
remembered.
A recent book on the College thus
describes the founding of Kenyon.
"Philander Chase came to Ohio in
the winter of 1818, traveling by
horse and sled over the ice and snow
of the wilderness. Elected first
Bishop of Ohio three years later, he
rode over a thousand miles within
twelve months, between times work
ing at his homestead like any pio
neer. Because the greatest need in
his work was trained men, he de
termined to open a college in the
West. Against all advice, but with
the sureness of purpose that marked
his whole life, he audaciously sailed
to England; by his personality and
earnestness won such distinguished
friends as Kenyon, Gambier, Bexley, and Lady Rosse to his cause;
and returned with Kenyon College
in his pocket in the form of about
thirty thousand dollars. Then he
chose the site and erected monu
mental Old Kenyon and Rosse Hall :
Kenyon College was a fact. And
Dr. Gobdon Keith Chalmers,
President of Kenyon College
through the years that immediately
followed, he guided the destinies of
the College so that it grew in sta
ture and influence At his death in
1852 he was Presiding Bishop of the
American Church."
Old in years, yet young in spirit
and policy, Kenyon perpetuated its
tradition of naming young men to
the presidency by inaugurating in
1937 Dr. Gordon Keith Chalmers as
its new president. He succeeded Wil-

There is approximately one pro

includes many names prominent

som, professor of poetry, was a

who is a graduate of Yale and Ox

Yale, he was a sprinter on the
United States Olympic Team in
1924.
For many decades Kenyon has
restricted its enrollment to 250 stu

applicants for admission has been
so large that the limit has been
raised to 300, at which figure the
enrollment now stands.

President Nicholas Murray Butler, Lambda '82, wrote for the
June, 1921, issue of The Diamond:
"In all the debates and the discussions as to the place of fra
ternities in American undergraduate life, too little emphasis is
placed on their value as a real instrument of education. When
one speaks of education, ordinarily merely instruction is meant;
but instruction by itself is but a small and shabby part of educa
tion. True education involves human contacts, broadening human
interests, and various free forms of human association, all of
which make the fruits of human instruction worth while, and
assist to apply instruction in useful and interesting ways. _
"The college fraternity is nothing more nor less than a highly
organizedform of human contact. It offers invitation and oppor
tunity to young men of like temperament and like tastes to live
together during undergraduate days, to be in close association
with each other, and through these contacts and associations to
develop each others' minds in a hundred ways that could not be
accomplished by instruction alone."

gram could not be announced at the

It is recorded that Williams Col
lege first knocked at the door of Psi
Upsilon-in 1874. The door, however,
failed to open to these early peti
tioners and thirty-nine years passed
before this outstanding New Eng
land college found Psi U numbered
among the leading national frater
nities represented on its campus. To
the Delta Delta Fraternity, founded
in 1911 for the express purpose of
bringing Psi U to Williams, went
the honor of being commissioned
with the task of establishing a firstclass chapter on a basis of equality
with the strong fraternities already
firmly entrenched at Williams. How
successfully they met this challenge
as the Delta Delta Chapter of Psi
Upsilon is told in the record of cam
pus leadership assumed by their
members during the first quarter
century of the Chapter's life.
In the founding of Delta Delta,
a prominent part was played by
Henry Wolcott Toll, '09, a member
of Kappa Alpha, who cherished the
idea of establishing at Williams the
fraternity of which his father and
two brothers were members. His
younger brother, Oliver, who en
tered college in the fall of 1909, was
enthused with the same idea. To
gether they laid the foundations of
Delta Delta and associated with
them the group of undergraduates,
many of them with Psi U connec
tions, who announced in the spring
of 1911 that a new fraternity had
come into being at Williams. The
news was favorably received on the
campus, due to the caliber of the
students who composed the new
group. S
By the time college opened in the
fall of 1911, the new fraternity had
acquired a splendid property of
eleven acres where a commodious
frame house with sleeping and study
accommodations for sixteen men
commanded a beautiful view of
"Berkshire's peerless hills." This
was easily the most attractive prop
erty in Williamstown and easily ac
cessible to the center of college
activities. Its value has grown with
the years as new college buildings
and athletic fields have made their
appearance in the direction of the
Psi U property.
As the demands of the active
chapter increased, the original
home, was replaced by a brick
structure of informal tudor archi
tecture, equaling in dignity and
charm, as well as spaciousness, any
of the fraternity houses at Williams
and indeed any of the Psi U homes
at other colleges. It was designed
by John T. Whitmore, Delta Delta
'16. The corner stone was laid on
June 19, 1926, and on February 19,
1927, the new home was dedicated
to Psi Upsilon.
Here Delta Delta's Twenty-fifth
Anniversary will be celebrated and
here the bonds of Psi U fellowship
renewed on May 7. Here, too, will
be relived in the memories of a
large gathering of Delta Delta
Alumni the days in which were laid
the foundations for those life-long
friendships which after all comprise
the richest heritage of fraternal life.

The Brothers returned from Christmas
vacation to find that Brother Hector
had been awarded a Rhodes Scholarship.
There have only been four Rhodes
Scholars selected from Williams in the
last ten years, and two of these are mem
bers of Psi Upsilon.
Brother Strong has been reelected
President with Brothers Hector, Boyn
ton, Coffin, McReynolds, Warden,
Whiteley, and Cooper fflling, respec
tively, the other house offices. Brother
Boynton has been chosen to fill the
position on the Undergraduate Council.
Brothers Coffin, Whiteley, Cook,and
Behrer are members of one of the strong
est swimming teams in the history of
Williams. Brother Coffin holds the pool
and college record in diving with a mark
he established last year. Brother Wells,
a sophomore, is one of the outstanding
players on the hockey team. Brother
Sowards is on the varsity basketball
squad. Pledge Stuart swims for the
freshman team while Pledge Conant is
a star member of the freshman hockey
sextet. The house has been doing ex
ceptionally well in interfraternity sports
this year, and at present is near the top
in the basketball league.
Brothers Strong, Boynton, Coffin,
and Cooper were appointed members of
the annual Chest Fund Drive. At the
present time Brother MUls, a member
of the Board of Directors of Cap and
Bells, the college dramatic organization,
is directing one of the three one-act
plays to be presented in the near future.
Brother Kaelber designed the set for
Brother Mills' play.
John A. Cooper,

EPSILON PHI
McGill University
With the election of new officers
Brother Dave Skelton has taken over
the presidency so ably held by Brother
Don MacCallum. Congratulations to
him. We also express our hearty appre
ciation to Brother Miles Gordon for
the excellent Chapter History which he
has recently compiled.
A precedent was established this year
when the Brothers had their mothers at
the house for an informal tea. A large
number of mothers attended, and, judg
ing from their remarks, they heartily
approve of the manner in which the
House is being run.
Plans are now afoot for the celebra
tion of the tenth anniversary of the
linking of Epsilon Phi and Psi Upsilon.
Many students were forced to leave the
University or drop courses after the
recent Christmas examinations, but the
Zeta Zeta, with a second class average
slightly higher than we have had for
some years, is still at full strength. We
hope to continue this improvement and
bring back the scholarship cup this
spring.
The fraternities all lost several pro
spective members through the ineligi
bility of several of the freshman class.
However, we are proud to report a suc
cessful campaign and the pledging of
eight men, making this year's delega
tion twelve strong. Since pledging rou
tine, campus life has been broken by
the Varsity Invasion to Victoria where
thirty of the Brothers and Alumni of
that city had an enjoyable luncheon.
Pledge training will culminate in an
initiation banquet on February 15,
It will probably be in the form of an
informal gathering in the House where
the active Brothers and the Alumni
alike will bow their heads over a barrel
of oysters. The date is March 17 and
any Brothers in the vicinity will be
most welcome.
The House hockey team easily won
its first game in the interfraternity
league and anticipates another success
ful season on the ice. The Brothers are
doing fairly well in college athletics.
Brother Mislap was one of the top
scorers when the senior basketball team
journeyed to Toronto and Western.
T. A. Harvie,
